name: Capacitor
summary: A web-native runtime that packages a built web application inside iOS and Android projects, synchronizes web assets and native dependencies, and exposes platform APIs through JavaScript plugins.

features.name: Built web bundle in a native shell
features.description: Capacitor takes the output of a web build and places it into native iOS and Android projects. The native shell hosts the web application while the project remains open to platform IDEs and native code.
benefits: Reuses web application code while producing installable mobile binaries
Keeps native project ownership available for platform-specific work
Makes the web asset directory an explicit input to the mobile runtime
costs: The web build must be complete and correctly configured before synchronization
Web and native lifecycle differences require integration testing
Native project and signing concerns remain outside the web toolchain

features.name: JavaScript-native plugin bridge
features.description: Capacitor plugins provide a JavaScript-facing interface to native APIs. The bridge dispatches plugin calls and events into platform implementations, while plugin guidance emphasizes small, unified, and idiomatic contracts across iOS and Android.
benefits: Exposes device capabilities through a web-oriented programming model
Allows native implementations to be packaged and shared as plugins
Creates an explicit boundary for platform value normalization and lifecycle
costs: Plugin APIs must reconcile differences in native platform behavior
Each plugin adds native code, permissions, and compatibility surface
Bridge calls and asynchronous events introduce lifecycle and failure modes

features.name: Sync-driven native dependency lifecycle
features.description: The Capacitor CLI sync operation copies built web assets into both native projects and installs or updates the native dependencies required by Capacitor. Subsequent run, open, and build operations use the synchronized native projects.
benefits: Makes web asset and native dependency propagation a repeatable command
Supports both IDE-driven and terminal/CI-driven native builds
Provides a checkpoint between web development and native compilation
costs: A stale or incorrect sync can produce a native binary that does not match web source
Dependency updates can trigger platform-specific build and compatibility failures
The lifecycle spans package management, native IDEs, and signing environments

mathematical_views.question: How do web application modules, bridge calls, plugin implementations, and host-platform APIs connect?
assumptions: Web modules and native implementations are distinct node classes
Plugin methods and events are typed bridge edges between the classes
The view abstracts WebView internals and platform API implementation details

mathematical_views.question: How does a web source change progress through build, synchronization, native execution, and distributable binary states?
assumptions: A built web asset directory is the input to synchronization
Sync copies assets and updates native dependencies before run or build
The model does not infer that a successful sync proves platform behavior or store acceptance

benefits: Web code can be distributed through platform-native application shells
costs: Web/native lifecycle and platform build constraints remain coupled at release time

benefits: A web-facing API can reach device capabilities through replaceable plugins
costs: Cross-platform normalization, permissions, and bridge failure handling add maintenance work

benefits: Asset and dependency propagation is explicit and repeatable
costs: Native dependency and toolchain failures become part of every synchronized release
